revision_review.requested_change: HYPOTHETICAL author-proposed counterfactual for a 30-Book architecture exercise. It is NOT an accepted amendment and must remain working and noncanonical. Apply counterfactual H1 and the witness-led repair R-A. H1: in Book 5 the Stone Hall's own head, Keeper Anselm Corrow, not the tenders, opens the sealed records as a reform to protect the Hall's standing against the spring's thinning; a lower-terrace household's evidence forces the timing; the Hall is reformed rather than destroyed; its committee keeps the debt reading; Dorran carries the reform as messenger rather than defecting. Reconsider every materially affected element: the Arc I phase, the Ledger and Stone Hall nodes, the custody thread, the anger/grief emotion targets, the political-institutional genre contract, and the Arc II and III phases where the reform's rules and partial readings now have authors. Preserve the fixed brief, the three loops (ledger-source, old-hand-ledger-source, openness-trade-source), the Arc II trade mechanism, the Book 15 gift reading and every unaffected decision. Do not add arbitrary antagonists or postpone revelations. Name the new open question the counterfactual creates.

changed_components.title: Governing summary
changed_components.before: The Spring Ledger (working, noncanonical): a terraced highland valley is watered from a glacier-fed spring. Water reaches the terraces only where its shares are recorded, and each share creates a labour return owed to the channels. Three co-governing engines interact: the Ledger (recorded shares and owed returns), the Source (the spring's physical balance, which rises or falls with the gap between draw and return and is not a character), and the Old Hand (the interpretive legitimacy that decides whether a return is a debt, a gift or a contract). The series' central question is who gives back the water and whether giving must be counted. Governing role rotates across five macro arcs (Reckoned Water, Books 1-5; The Turn, 6-11; The Old Hand, 12-18; Settled Water, 19-22; Unmeasured, 23-30). Each arc ends in a changed governing engine, and each victory changes institutions (Stone Hall, Terrace Council, Mill Compact, Reading Hall) that act from their own agency. Renewal comes from feasibility, distribution and legitimacy pressures generated by earlier outcomes, not from escalating antagonists. Nothing here is accepted Identity, Structure or Book canon; the fixed author brief is the only fixed input.

changed_components.title: Evidence that forces reform
changed_components.after: A lower-terrace household's record and its wild channel force the Hall to open its records. Evidence, not seizure, is the protagonist's lever. Added by revision R-A.

changed_components.title: Ledger engine
changed_components.before: Recorded shares set the draw. Credit can be falsified or favoured (Book 1), opened (Book 5), traded (Book 6), and re-read as gift or contract (Book 15). Each change alters who must return labour.
changed_components.after: Recorded shares set the draw. Credit can be falsified or favoured (Book 1), opened by the Hall's own reform once evidence forces it (Book 5), traded under the reform's rules (Book 6), and re-read as gift or contract (Book 15). Each change alters who must return labour.

changed_components.title: Stone Hall (reform committee and remnant)
changed_components.before: Hereditary keepers of the Ledger. Acts from its own agency: dissolves in Book 5 but a remnant under Keeper Corrow continues as a dissenting institution (typed as other because v2 has no institution category).
changed_components.after: Hereditary keepers of the Ledger. Keeper Corrow opens the sealed records as a reform (Book 5) after household evidence forces the timing. The committee keeps the debt reading to protect its own legitimacy, and Dorran carries the reform as messenger. The Hall is reformed, not destroyed.

changed_components.title: Custody of the record
changed_components.before: Who holds the Ledger and on whose authority. Custody is the Stone Hall's source of legitimacy until Book 5 and contested afterwards.
changed_components.after: Who holds the Ledger and on whose authority. Custody passes from a sealed house to a reform committee (Book 5) and then to a plural body (Book 15 onward).

changed_components.title: inst_stone_hall -> eng_old_hand
changed_components.after: the reform committee keeps the debt reading to protect its own legitimacy

changed_components.title: th_witness -> inst_stone_hall
changed_components.after: evidence forces the reform's timing and proof

changed_components.title: Reckoned Water
changed_components.before: The Ledger governs. Stone Hall credit is proven false; a lower terrace runs wild; the Hall's monopoly breaks at a local cost. Book 1 gives the first partial reading of the First Stones. Protagonist's agency comes from evidence and a coalition, not inheritance. | Reader experience: wonder at the first hidden chamber under the spring; anger at falsified credit | Transition: Records open, so shares become tradable and the spring shows its first recorded thinning.
changed_components.after: The Ledger governs. A lower-terrace household's record exposes falsified credit and a wild channel (Book 1). The Stone Hall's head, Keeper Corrow, opens the sealed records as a reform to protect the Hall's standing against thinning (Book 5), but only after the household's evidence forces the timing. The Hall is reformed, not destroyed; its committee keeps the debt reading. Dorran carries the reform as messenger rather than defecting. | Reader experience: wonder at the first hidden chamber under the spring; anger at falsified credit | Transition: Records open, so shares become tradable; the reform committee, not the tenders, sets the first rules of sale.

changed_components.title: The Turn
changed_components.before: The Source governs. Open records make shares a commodity. The Compact's purchases draw water without return labour, so the physical balance is the constraint that decides what the institutions can do. Partial reading of the First Stones (Book 8) makes the Old Hand contested knowledge. | Reader experience: belonging tested by sale; anger at a market in shares | Transition: Maintenance becomes an institution (the Turn) and the Old Hand becomes disputed knowledge.
changed_components.after: The Source governs. The reform's sale rules let the Mill Compact buy shares; draw separates from return and the upper cistern thins (Book 6). Quillmark's tenders and the Terrace Council oppose rules the reform committee approved. Partial readings of the Stones (Book 8) are authored by the committee and contested by scholars. | Reader experience: belonging tested by sale; anger at a market in shares | Transition: Maintenance becomes an institution (the Turn) and the Old Hand becomes disputed knowledge.

changed_components.title: The Old Hand
changed_components.before: The Old Hand governs. Legitimacy no longer rests on the Ledger alone. The Unmeasured Return is a costly, physically consequential choice: it stabilises the lower valley and disturbs the high cistern. The Reading Hall is founded as a public institution with its own readings. | Reader experience: wonder that the first compact was not a debt; fear of the surfeit | Transition: Legitimacy is contested among three readings; no single institution holds the record.
changed_components.after: The Old Hand governs. The complete reading of the First Stones (Book 15) makes the first compact a gift. The reform committee must now choose between its legitimacy as the debt-keeping Hall and the gift reading that would undo it; the Council and the Compact press their readings. The Unmeasured Return is tried in Lower Ammen; its surfeit in the high terraces forces a stewardship tally. The Reading Hall is founded. | Reader experience: wonder that the first compact was not a debt; fear of the surfeit | Transition: Legitimacy is contested among three readings; no single institution holds the record.

changed_components.title: anger · supporting
changed_components.before: outrage at credit falsified against the powerless | Elicited by: the falsified lower-terrace share in Book 1
changed_components.after: unease that an institution must be forced into correcting itself, and that its correction still costs the wronged | Elicited by: the falsified lower-terrace share in Book 1, and the committee's partial correction in Book 5

changed_components.title: gn_political_institutional
changed_components.before: Role: supporting; engine: institutions compete for legitimacy over who may keep and read the record; structure: arcs alternate between custody disputes and distribution disputes
changed_components.after: Role: supporting; engine: institutions reform or resist from within; legitimacy is contested by people who once held it; structure: arcs alternate between custody disputes and distribution disputes
